newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Hochtief and Holzmann bet on Brussels.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hochtief and Holzmann bet on Brussels.

text.p: Germany's two largest construction groups, Philipp Holzmann AG and Hochtief AG, on Tuesday gave details of a cooperation pact which they said will not require the approval of the German cartel authorities.

Announcing a pact under which Hochtief's 24.9 percent stake will be "pooled" with a 25.1 percent interest held by banking giant Deutsche Bank, the groups involved said the particularities of the arrangement meant it could only be vetted by European competition authorities.

But they insisted that the agreement was not an attempt to sidestep the German Federal Cartel Office that for more than two years has blocked efforts by Hochtief to increase its stake and influence in the larger Holzmann group.
"This plan must be seen as a whole new start. The fact that we must now go to Brussels is a completely new development," Deutsche Bank board member Carl von Boehm-Bezing told a news conference.
Boehm-Bezing nonetheless added that certain "legal advantages" pertained to the new arrangement which Hochtief's earlier efforts to increase its Holzmann stake to 35 percent clearly did not possess.

The deal is initially intended to allow Holzmann and Hochtief to cooperate in international markets before they go on to explore whether synergies in their domestic market are available and permissable.

Hochtief said such cooperation was an inevitable part of the somewhat late restructuring of the German construction sector, currently suffering from price pressure and stagnant demand which has resulted in deep unemployment.
"We are undergoing changes in the German market which have happened elswhere a long time ago," Hochtief chairman Hans-Peter Keitel told the news briefing.
"Pure construction will become more and more the domain of the small and medium companies, while companies of our size will work more as large project managers," he said.

Typical areas where cooperation between the two could be imagined would be on public infrastructure projects like the mooted German high-speed rail network or large road schemes, often involving private finance, he said.
Holzmann chief Lothar Mayer said that assuming approval of the pact, the two would start by examining each others relative strengths in international markets.
"We for example are strong in America and Asia and Hochtief is strong in Europe and South Africa," he said.

But the German cartel office issued a statement saying that the share pool raised "serious questions regarding competition" in the domestic German market and said it wanted to regain responsibility for the case.

"We shall request that the European Commission turns responsibility for this case back to the German Federal Cartel Office, because the case needs to be dealt with in the area where it has greatest impact -- Germany," cartel office president Dieter Wolf said.
He added that German companies continued to dominate the domestic construction market, with foreign groups having a market share of below 10 percent.
Under the envisaged pooling arrangement, the voting rights of both shareholdings, totalling some 50 percent, will be exercised jointly at annual shareholder meetings.

A joint statement by the three groups said that the two construction firms would retain their separate identity under the pact, which is due to last for at least 10 years, and that there were no plans for a merger of the two.

Despite the size of the companies involved in the deal -- which would of itself make the European competition authorities responsible for vetting it -- the German cartel office could have retained responsibility if all three parties made more than two-thirds of their European revenues in Germany.

While that was the case for Hochtief and Holzmann, the cartel office said, it accepted that this was not true for Deutsche -- which sources more than a third of its European revenues outside its domestic market.

Assuming the approval of Brussels, Hochtief will give up its efforts to acquire a further 10 percent stake in Holzmann -- now parked with Commerzbank AG -- which is currently the object of a German appeal court study.
Holzmann shares were traded 17 marks up at 550 marks in post-bourse trade, while Hochtief was up 80 pfennigs at 72.20 marks.
